Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. The founder and first president of the modern Turkish Republic. Atatürk led Turkish forces to victory in the Turkish War of Independence from nineteen nineteen to nineteen twenty-three against occupying Allied powers and Greek invasion. He abolished the Ottoman sultanate in nineteen twenty-two and established the Turkish Republic in nineteen twenty-three, declaring himself president. Atatürk implemented radical secularizing reforms: he closed religious schools, replaced Islamic law with European legal codes, and separated religion from state affairs. In nineteen twenty-eight, he adopted the Latin alphabet in place of Arabic script, modernizing education and literacy despite fierce opposition. He changed the nation's name from Ottoman Empire to Turkey, promoting Turkish nationalism and a modern, Western-oriented identity. He granted women's suffrage and legal equality in nineteen thirty-four, ahead of many European nations. When he died in nineteen thirty-eight, he was revered as the architect of modern Turkey. His remains lie in the Anıtkabir, a monument in Ankara that stands as a symbol of his legacy. His reforms influenced later leaders across the Middle East, exemplifying the creation of a modern nationalist state from the remnants of empire.
